q-32550.name: Question 1
q-32550.problem:
Given that 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}]$ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
q-32550.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+5{R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Given that A=[1−2−56] has the LU decomposition A=LU, then L=

a

[10−21]

[10−51]
d

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

A=[1−2−56]R2:=R2+5R1⟺[1051]⏞E1⋅A∼[1−20−4]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[1051]−1UA=[10−51]⏟L[1−20−4]⏟U

q-32619.name: Question 2
q-32619.problem:
Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 8 & -12\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU$, then ${l}_{21}+{u}_{22}=$
q-32619.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 8 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{21}=4,{u}_{22}=0,$ and ${l}_{21}+{u}_{22}=4.$

Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

A=[2−38−12]R2:=R2+(−4)R1⟺[10−41]⏞E1⋅A∼[2−300]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[10−41]−1UA=[1041]⏟L[2−300]⏟U.

Therefore, l21=4,u22=0, and l21+u22=4.

q-74951.name: Question 3
q-74951.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}].$ 
has the LU decomposition $A=LU$, then $L=$
q-74951.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{4}{3}{R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{4}{3} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{4}{3} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -\frac{4}{3} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices: A=[32−4−3]R2:=R2+43R1⟺[10431]⏞E1⋅A∼[320−13]=U

q-106760.name: Question 4
q-106760.problem:
Given that 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -16 & 10\end{aligned}]$ 
has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
q-106760.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -16 & 10\end{aligned}] & \,{R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-8){R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -8 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 8 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

q-106773.name: Question 5
q-106773.problem:
Given that
$A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]$
has the LU decomposition $A=LU$, then ${l}_{21}+{u}_{22}=$
q-106773.worked_solution:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1}\,⟺\,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since ${E}_{1}A=U,$ we can invert ${E}_{1}$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -\frac{2}{3} & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${l}_{21}=-\frac{2}{3},$ ${u}_{22}=0,$ and ${l}_{21}+{u}_{22}=-\frac{2}{3}.$

Question 5
?

Given that A=[3−6−24] has the LU decomposition A=LU, then l21+u22=

a
−23
b
−13
c
13
d
23
e
−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the matrices L and U, we reduce the matrix A to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to A in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices:

A=[3−6−24]R2:=R2+(23)R1⟺[10231]⏞E1⋅A∼[3−600]=U

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix U. Now, since E1A=U, we can invert E1 to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

E1A=UA=E1−1UA=[10231]−1UA=[10−231]⏟L[3−600]⏟U

Therefore, l21=−23, u22=0, and l21+u22=−23.
